newsitem.title: USA: U.S. ends probe of Tenet who may head CIA.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ends probe of Tenet who may head CIA.

text.p: The Justice Department has ended its investigation of George Tenet, President Bill Clinton's choice to head the CIA, clearing the way for Senate action on his nomination, administration officials said on Wednesday.

They said the U.S. Justice Department finished its preliminary investigation into Tenet's failure to disclose certain stock and real estate holdings, deciding not to seek the appointment of an independent counsel.

The decision cleared the way for a Senate committee to vote on Tenet's nomination as director of central intelligence, the officials said, adding that the committee wanted to wait for the investigation to end before taking any action.

Clinton tapped Tenet for the chief spymaster job after a bruising fight with Senate Republicans over his initial choice of Anthony Lake, the president's first-term national security adviser who withdrew his nomination for the CIA post.

Tenet's nomination seemed likely to sail through the Senate Intelligence Committee until the Justice Department began investigating his failure to disclose his part-interest in stocks and real estate inherited from his father.
The Justice Department under the law has 90 days to conduct a preliminary investigation to determine if an independent counsel should be appointed.

In his current job as deputy director of the CIA, Tenet is covered by the law. The deadline for the investigation to be finished was July 20. Attorney General Janet Reno approved the decision not to seek an independent counsel, the officials said.

At issue were telephone stock and condominium apartments in Greece Tenet inherited from his father, who died in 1983, but that Tenet did not list on his initial financial disclosure forms when he joined the Clinton administration.

Tenet, previously a senior intelligence adviser on the White House National Security Council staff from 1993 to 1995, said he did not learn about the stock and the Athens property until 1994, when his brother discovered their existence after looking through a family safe deposit box.

Justice Department investigators doubted from the start that there would be sufficient evidence to warrant an independent counsel, but felt compelled by law to conduct a thorough investigation to make sure, the officials said.
Committee leaders were told on Tuesday of the Justice Department's conclusion, with formal notification possibly coming as soon as Wednesday, the officials said.
